pages.name: Planetside Procedures
pages.html:
Planetside Procedures

Planetside Procedures: There are four 6-hour intervals to track per typical planetside day. This is used to determine when to make encounter checks, how to track travel, and how to track the time needed to complete tasks. On planets that have significant time differences by -6 or +6 hours per day, add or subtract an interval. The following example is using a typical 24-hour day rotation.

  • Morning: 6:00 -12:00
  • Afternoon: 12:00 - 18:00
  • Evening: 18:00 - 0:00
  • Night: 0:00 - 6:00

Humans are adapted to a 24hr day, so while they might be on planets with more or fewer hours than they are adapted to, they will still frequently function within 6-hour blocks of activity (travel, building, crafting, repairing, etc.) and non-activity (resting, recovering, etc.) to best suit their needs.

Planetside Encounter Checks:

  • While stationary: One encounter check per day.
  • While travelling: One encounter check per 6-hour shift of travelling OR change of terrain/environment.

Book p.96

pages.name: Weather
pages.html:
Weather

Weather Checks: Make a weather check every 6-hour interval. Depending on the planet’s temperature, use the following table to modify the weather table based on the temperature zone the traveler is located in on the planet. Listed below are the different temperature zones, with earth analogues listed in parentheses.

  • Above Average (Tropical): 25% above or below the planet’s equator
  • Average Zone (Temperate): 50% above or below the Above Average zone
  • Below Average (Polar): 25% above or below the Average Zone, in an area that encompasses the planet’s poles

Temperature Dice Modification should be applied to the following:

  • Encounter Checks
  • Survival Checks
  • Weather Check

  • Vehicle movement penalty: this is the decrease in vehicle movement speed in addition to the terrain penalty.

Book p.96-97

pages.name: Overland Travel
pages.html:
Overland Travel

Overland Walking Travel: The typical human can walk 30km in six hours when not hindered by terrain and weather.

  • 1 Hour: 5 km
  • 3 Hours: 15 km
  • 6 Hours: 30 km

Overland Vehicle Travel: Vehicles will have variable travel speeds that can impact how far and how difficult it is to drive them in different terrain and weather.

Overland Vehicle Speed: In Spacer, vehicles are listed with their top speed described as a speed band, but it is not advisable to only travel at top speed, due to the dangers that may arise. Use the following speed band changes to determine the difficulty of Drive checks when travelling overland.

  • Speed Band 0: if a Speed Band modifier causes the speed to drop to zero, then the vehicle is considered to be stopped.
  • Cruise Speed: Cruise speed for a vehicle is the average speed the vehicle is operated at. Operating a vehicle at cruise speed in conditions that wouldn’t cause difficulty doesn’t require any checks to operate.
  • Difficulty: The listed difficulty is when the vehicle is on a road or level surface. Terrain modifiers that decrease the speed band don't have an effect on the difficulty. However, if a vehicle’s speed band will take a penalty of -3 out of 4, then to move at Speed 1 will be equal to driving at top gear due to the hazards of the terrain.
  • Result of failure: The result of failure will determine the continued functionality of the vehicle.
  • Injury: When a crash occurs, any passengers onboard may be subjected to harm. Each passenger takes 1D of damage per speed band. If colliding into another vehicle head-on, then the damage is equal to both vehicle’s speed bands added together. Passengers ejected from the vehicle are tossed out at 5 m per speed band, starting at Speed Band 3.
Vehicle SpeedSpeed Band DecreaseDM to the RollResult of Failure
Low Gear-3+2 DMFender bender, cosmetic damage
Mid Gear-2+1 DMMinor crash, hull damage
High Gear-1+0 DMCrash, critical damage
Top Gear-0-2 DMSevere crash, inoperable until repaired

Skilled Drivers: Overland vehicles with speeds higher than 200kmh (Speed Band 4) require the Drive Skill, with every +1 rank being applied to an increase in total speed band they can operate at.

Example of a vehicle’s speed band by speed range: A ground car, with a speed band of 4 (200 kmh)—

  • Low Gear: Speed Band 1 (20 kmh)
  • Mid Gear: Speed Band 2 (50 kmh)
  • High Gear: Speed Band 3 (100 kmh), cruise speed
  • Top Gear: Speed Band 4 (200 kmh), max speed

Roads: Driving on roads will decrease the difficulty DM by -1 due to terrain and speed. Paved roads decrease the DM by -2.

*Indicates attempts to survive with damaged/inadequate equipment. Example: Damaged vaccsuit, compromised air filter/rebreather, lack of scuba fins, etc.

Terrain Description:

  • Open Country: This represents mostly level and unobstructed terrain with minimal to sporadic landscape features.
  • Shrubland: This is terrain that has significant overgrowth of plant life, such as grass, moss, brambles, clumps of trees, and bushes.
  • Wetland: Wetlands are semi-aquatic shrubland made up of swamps, bogs, river basins, estuaries, and other water features, which is rich with a significant amount of plant life.
  • Arctic: This is an extremely cold environment that is significantly frigid open country, mountains, and shrubland. Arctic environments typically have significant amounts of snow and ice that restrict travel and survivability.
  • Desert: Deserts are extremely hot and arid open country with malleable surfaces that makes travel difficult and arduous. Deserts may have occasional geological formations, with the chance of an oasis to provide respite.
  • Mountainous: This includes mountains and other significant geological formations that obstruct overland travel but are also notable environments for plants and animals. Mountains tend to have more extreme weather and temperature changes as they are climbed, which may apply -1DM to any survival checks per vertical 500m increment climbed.
  • Aquatic: Aquatic environments are locations that are mostly or all water, such as oceans, archipelagos, inland seas, etc. Humans cannot easily traverse aquatic environments without vehicles or proper equipment; otherwise they risk drowning.
  • Vacuum: This type of terrain is normally devoid of life. It will be similar to open country and mountainous terrain but will have locations of extremely jagged and dangerous geological formations due to the lack of a notable atmosphere to provide erosion. This type of environment requires functional equipment for humans to explore.

Book p.98

pages.html:
Planetside Encounters

Planetside Encounter Check: Use the table below to determine when an encounter check is made based on where on a planet you’re currently located. This roll is modified by the modifier in the Encounter Type DM column.

  • To make an encounter check: Roll 1D and apply Terrain Type DM. A result of 6+ is an encounter.
  • Determine encounter type: If an encounter occurs, roll 2D and consult the Encounter Type Table. Apply the Encounter Type DM to this roll.
LocationCheck FrequencyEncounter Chance & Type DMPlanetside Encounter Table Roll

  • Check frequency: This is the typical amount of times an encounter check is made. If a planet has more or less hours than 24hrs in a day, round up or down by 6 hours for every 4 hour difference from 24 hours. A check frequency should never be less than 6 hours.
  • Encounter chance & type DM: Apply this DM along with any weather DM to the Encounter Chance and the Encounter Type Table.
  • Encounter Tables roll: Use the listed dice type to determine what is encountered on the Planetside Encounter or Planetside Location Encounter Table.
  • UWC Population Code: This is the DM to the tens place on a d36 or d66 roll, as determined by the population type of the world.

Encounter Types:

  • NPC Encounter: This is when a human, animal, or something else living is encountered. Use the NPC interaction table to determine how they react to the spacer.
  • Location Encounter: This means coming across structures, groups of animals, robots, and other interactive elements that dot the landscape, etc. By default, encounters aren’t helpful or hostile. Determine the encounter’s reaction to the spacer using the NPC reaction table.
  • Environment: Environment encounters are situational scenarios dictated by the location the spacer is in, which they can choose to interact with or may have to deal with.

Habitat Conditions

Habitat Condition: If a result of 41-62 on the Planetside Location table is rolled, roll 2D in each column on the following table and apply the Encounter Chance & Type DM to the roll. This will determine how it looks from a distance and any clues as to what it is.

2DOccupiedCondition
1 or lessAbandoned andDestroyed/collapsed
2-3AbandonedFalling apart/ overgrown

5-9In useShowing age/ weathered
10Occupied butUnder construction/being repaired
11-12OccupiedWell-maintained
13+Occupied andFortified
  • Abandoned: This location appears to be not in use or operational.
  • In use: This location is operational and clearly indicates who owns and operates the location.
  • Occupied: This location is operational, but it is unclear who owns and operates the location and what the habitat’s function is.

Book p.101

pages.name: Settlement Encounters
pages.html:
Settlement Encounters

Settlement Encounters: Every six hours (or every 1D hours) spent exploring a settlement, an encounter occurs. A settlement encounter is generated by roll a D66 on the encounter table.

  • Legal Encounters: Once per day, including on entry into the settlement roll 2D; if the roll is under the local law level then the encounter is a legal encounter. This represents law enforcement asking for paperwork, frisking spacers, or custom officers searching the spacer's starship. Use the NPC demeanour table (pg.56) to determine how they engage with the spacers.
  • Settlement encounter modification: The encounter table is modified by the world population and local law level. Consult the following table to determine the combined DM to use with the Settlement Encounter Table.

Settlement Encounter Modification Table: Use the planet’s UWC codes to determine any Dice Modifications. The DM is applied to the tens place of the d66 roll.

Pop SizeDMLaw LevelDM

6-7-14-5+2
8-9+06-8+3
10(A)++19++4

Settlement Encounter Table: Determine the total DM, then roll D66, applying the DM to the tens place.

  • Random NPCs: Generate the random NPC using the Random NPC Table (pg.58), using the range stated in the Settlement Encounter result. Use the NPC demeanour table on pg. 56, with SOC DM applied to determine their reaction to the spacer and their crew.

This table is designed to reflect the condition of the settlement:

  • 01 - 06: Abandoned or neglected
  • 11 - 16: Seedy
  • 21 - 26: Rundown
  • 31 - 36: Out of date
  • 41 - 46: Maintained
  • 51 - 56: Burgeoning
  • 61 - 66: Esteemed
  • 71 - 76: Decline
  • 81 - 86: Dystopian
  • 91 - 96: Oppressive

Planetside Colonies: If exploring a planet that isn’t the primary world of the star system, then settlements encountered are considered colonies of that main world. A colony is a sponsored settlement created to establish a foothold in a new location. This usually is designed to develop a community around an industry, incentive program, or ideological reasons.

Planetside Environment Encounters

Avoiding Environmental Encounters: In the case of any planetside environment encounters that the travellers want to avoid, it will take 6 hours to travel around them on foot, while any dangerous weather changes will take 1D days to pass by.
